title: Andy Burnham to address social care, youth unemployment and devolution
description: The source said: "He has the courage to fix the most difficult issues that have been ignored for years and seen as impossible to resolve. He doesn't a
body: The source said: "He has the courage to fix the most difficult issues that have been ignored for years and seen as impossible to resolve. He doesn't accept that they are. They can't be ignored any longer."The prime minister is determined to show that governments can make people's lives better if they choose to. He wants to get Britain believing again."Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use, and people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with the cost of care from their local council.Burnham would not be the first leader in recent years to pledge to address the issue of adult social care. In 2019, in his first speech as prime minister, Boris Johnson said the Conservative Party would "fix the crisis in social care once and for all".Five years later in July 2024, Keir Starmer faced criticism when Labour scrapped plans for an £86,000 cap on the amount anyone in England would need to spend on their personal care over their lifetime. Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey, who has pushed for social care reform, said on Saturday:  "This has to be the start of a real effort to end the social care catastrophe."He added: "I'll fight to ensure family carers aren't forgotten. We need cross-party consensus, and I hope the PM's door is open."Burnham responded to Sir Ed on X, writing: "It most certainly is, Ed. Let's work together to find some common ground."Kevin Hollinrake, chairman of the Conservative Party, said: "Where's the money coming from, Andy? We're all dying to know."It is all well and good for the prime minister to promise to fix the issues facing our country, but how is he going to pay for them?"In the first week of his premiership, Burnham has pledged to end rough sleeping in England, cut VAT from domestic electricity bills in the current financial year, and reduce the cap on bus fares outside of London from £3 to £2 from January.His government also announced it would cut business rates for pubs, clubs, and live music venues in England by 20% from April.

title: Clapham stabbing: Six men arrested over murder of 22-year-old man
description: Six men have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a 22-year-old man was fatally stabbed in Clapham, south-west London, the Metropolitan Police h
body: Six men have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a 22-year-old man was fatally stabbed in Clapham, south-west London, the Metropolitan Police has said.Police were called at 04:37 BST following reports of a man attending hospital with a stab wound. He later died in hospital, the force said.The incident is believed to have taken place around Tremadoc Road and Clapham High Street.Police said four of the suspects also attended hospital with stab wounds and are continuing to receive treatment, although their injuries are not believed to be life-threatening or life-changing.Alongside the four men in hospital – three aged 22 and one 24 – officers also arrested two further men, aged 27 and 23, at the hospital on suspicion of murder. They remain in police custody.The Met said it understood the fatally injured man was stabbed at about 04:20. It added that officers were carrying out inquiries in and around Tremadoc Road and Clapham High Street to establish the full circumstances around the incident.Det Ch Insp Sarah Lee, who is leading the investigation, said those in the area would continue to notice an increased police presence throughout Saturday.The family of the man who died have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.Supt Mark Gallacher, a policing lead for the area, described the incident as "tragic"."We understand that this will cause concern among the local community and specialist detectives are doing everything possible to determine what has happened," he added.The Met urged witnesses or people with information about the incident to contact police on 101, quoting reference 1474/25July.Information can also be provided anonymously to independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Vozinha: Cape Verde goalkeeper to join Chilean club Colo Colo after 2026 World Cup heroics
description: Vozinha, the Cape Verde goalkeeper who earned plaudits for his World Cup performances, is set to join Chilean side Colo Colo.The 40-year-old headed to
body: Vozinha, the Cape Verde goalkeeper who earned plaudits for his World Cup performances, is set to join Chilean side Colo Colo.The 40-year-old headed to the World Cup without a club after his contract with Portuguese second division side Chaves expired, but he became an overnight sensation by starring in a goalless draw against eventual champions Spain.He has now found a new club, according to Colo Colo president Anibal Mosa."Vozinha will be a Colo Colo player," said Mosa."In the coming days he will travel to Chile, undergo the usual medical examinations and then be presented here at the Estadio Monumental."Mosa said Vozinha's World Cup displays showed he deserved the move, acknowledging the signing also carried marketing appeal for Colo Colo.The club, based in the Chilean capital of Santiago, sit top of Liga de Primera - the country's top division.

title: Trump takes swipes at press during White House Correspondents' Dinner
description: In her remarks, WHCA President Weijia Jiang of CBS News said the event would return to the scene of the April shooting, the Washington Hilton, next ye
body: In her remarks, WHCA President Weijia Jiang of CBS News said the event would return to the scene of the April shooting, the Washington Hilton, next year. Friday's rescheduled event was held at the Waldorf Astoria a few miles away from that site, following criticisms that security at the Hilton was inadequate. The outgoing WHCA head said she would "refuse to let an act of violence have the final word", referring to the gunman tackled at the first dinner in April.The officer shot at the scene, officer Victor Gonzalez of the US Secret Service, was given an award by Trump for his actions on the night of the shooting."As I said three months ago, the show must go on," Trump said."Just like my presidency, the second time is always better – and the third time will be better yet … I'm only kidding," Trump said, joking that he would run for a third term in office. Trump stood and shook hands with award winners, including a Wall Street Journal team who was given an award for coverage of Trump's links to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.Ahead of the event, many in the White House press corps theorised that Trump - who often criticises many of the reporters seated just metres away in the room - would deliver a stern rebuke of the media.Trump's speech included pointed insults directed at several journalists, some of whom were in the room. The harsher tone and personal attacks extended to Democratic politicians and celebrities as his hour-long speech also took aim at familiar targets.But the US president also called on Americans to respect freedom of speech."We settle our differences not with bullets, but with open and vigorous debate," Trump said. "And no deranged loser with a gun will ever change that. We can't let that ever happen."Trump appeared to be in a good mood throughout the event, jokingly telling the media that "sometimes I really do think that some of you don't like me"."This place [the dinner] is really the largest group of 'Trump derangement syndrome' people ever put together at one time," he said. "I suspect some of you are lucky that our last dinner was cut short...I was going to go after you."The president joked the news industry would "be broke" after he leaves office because "there's not going to be anybody to report on", before putting on a Trump 2028 hat and saying he would run for another term."I'm pleased to announce my intention to, and this is somewhat of a scoop, my intention to run for a fourth term as president of the United States," Trump joked, apparently meaning he would run a fourth time. Since his second term began, Trump has repeatedly suggested he would run for a third term, despite the 22nd Amendment of the US Constitution mandating a two-term limit. The amendment was ratified in 1951 after President Franklin D Roosevelt served four consecutive terms. Trump has campaigned for president three times, and won two of the elections.The gala dinner came as relations between the White House and the media remain fraught. Last week, Trump threatened to revoke the licences of several US networks which did not carry his primetime speech about election security. The event was considerably scaled down from the first correspondents' dinner, with about 700 people in attendance, compared with more than 2,000 in April.Security was also tighter. Several blocks around the hotel were blocked off, with a heavy presence of police and national guard. Guests were screened twice, with QR codes and IDs, and were given wristbands.At one point, visitors were prompted to walk in a single file line past two Secret Service officers holding rifles.The suspect of the shooting in April, identified as 31-year-old Cole Tomas Allen, has been charged with attempting to assassinate the president of the United States. He was tackled by agents just short of a staircase which leads down to a ballroom where the dinner was getting underway.Others in attendance on Saturday night included Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

schema.headline: Trump takes swipes at press during White House Correspondents' Dinner

title: Two murder arrests follow Luton fatal stabbing
description: Two teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of murder after the fatal stabbing of a 17-year-old boy in Luton.Officers were called to reports of v
body: Two teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of murder after the fatal stabbing of a 17-year-old boy in Luton.Officers were called to reports of violent disorder in Kingsway Recreation Ground at about 18:30 on Friday, where a number of teenagers were seen carrying large knives.The 17-year-old, who has not been identified, was taken to hospital with multiple stab wounds but was pronounced dead shortly after, said Bedfordshire Police.One of the teenage boys, initially arrested on suspicion of violent disorder, remains in police custody. The second boy is in hospital with serious but non-life threatening injuries.In a statement, Det Ch Insp Nick Gardener condemned the "horrific violence" that has "sadly cost a teenage boy his life today"."Our thoughts are first and foremost with the loved ones of the boy who lost his life in such tragic circumstances," he said.Such incidents have "a significant impact on our communities", he said.He also urged the public to contact police with any information they have and not to share any images and videos circulating on social media.An increased police presence and patrols will remain in the area."We would also like to remind the public to not share any distressing videos or images as this can be concerning for family involved, and also form a vital part of our police investigation," he said.Zanib Raja, a councillor for the Biscot Ward in Luton, also asked people not to share alleged videos of the incident online. In a statement on Facebook, she said: "A tragic incident took place today in Kingsway Park, a place many of us grew up in, played in, and built memories in."A place that should be safe for families, children, and every resident of our town. Instead, a man lost his life in broad daylight. A family has been shattered. Luton is hurting."Raja urged the community to come together.

schema.headline: Two murder arrests follow Luton fatal stabbing

title: Peterborough farm's delight after six white owlets found nesting
description: Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, The owlets were ringed on Thursday by Simon DudhillByShariqua AhmedCambridgeA nest of six barn owlets has br
body: Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, The owlets were ringed on Thursday by Simon DudhillByShariqua AhmedCambridgeA nest of six barn owlets has brought good news to a farm after a challenging period.The fluffy birds - which are estimated to be between 40 to 50 days old - were discovered at Moor Farm, near Peterborough, and were ringed on Thursday as part of ongoing conservation work.Judith Jacobs, the farm's owner, said the owlets were thriving and had lifted spirits after the farm was the target of six suspected arson attacks this summer.Simon Dudhill, who monitors the birds for Peterborough City Council's barn owl recovery scheme, said finding six owlets sharing a nest was "exceptionally good" and was the largest brood he had encountered in 2026.He added he had ringed more than 260 owlets in Cambridgeshire this year. Each bird from Moor Farm was fitted with a metal ring carrying a unique identification number issued by the British Trust for Ornithology. The ring's details allow conservationists to track individual birds and provides information about their movements. Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, Simon Dudhill said finding six owlets together was "exceptionally good"Jacobs said: "It's very exciting as we had none last year. We try and encourage wildlife as much as we can. "We have created a lot of hunting paths for the owls away from the main road, so they can hunt safely, because the biggest predators for barn owls are cars."She said the six owlets, which include three females and three males, are each about three days apart in age."Simon measured the length of their fourth feather, which tells their age, and from the colour of their feathers, if they are spotty they are females and the non-spotty ones are males," she added. Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, The six owlets are each about three days apart in age and include three males and three femalesDudhill, who works for the Wildlife Conservation Partnership, external, said 2026 had been a much stronger breeding year for barn owls."I have ringed quite a few groups of five and four owlets this year. But this is the first  brood of six I have found," he added."Over the last couple of years, we have seen a decline in the number of babies but not adult barn owls. "Last year we found a lot of adults in boxes but they did not breed. This is all related to food. If there isn't enough food around, then they don't breed. "This year has been completely different. I personally found barn owl numbers have increased dramatically. But there are still some areas in Cambridgeshire that have not found as many babies as I have," he said. Despite monitoring barn owls for 15 years, Dudhill said the experience "never gets boring"."When you open a box, you have one or two or three little faces looking at you. It's just as exciting now as the first time I opened a box," he added. Do you have a story suggestion for Peterborough? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice

title: BuzzBallz are 'greenwashing' say recycling experts
description: BuzzBallz was founded by teacher Merrilee Kick, but was bought by the Sazerac Company, whose CEO is Jake Wenz, in 2024.BuzzBallz's UK's mission statem
body: BuzzBallz was founded by teacher Merrilee Kick, but was bought by the Sazerac Company, whose CEO is Jake Wenz, in 2024.BuzzBallz's UK's mission statement, which was deleted after the BBC contacted the company about this story, said it "loves our planet as much as we love a good cocktail" and partnered with TerraCycle to ensure its packaging gets recycled. However, TerraCycle, which involves consumers collecting packaging and sending it to be recycled, only runs the BuzzBallz scheme in the United States. BuzzBallz's UK FAQs, now also deleted, stated: "Yes, our packaging is recyclable. Please recycle your empties where local facilities allow."But no local facilities anywhere in the UK allow BuzzBallz to be recycled, said Adam Herriott, the head of packaging at WRAP."They're a mix of two very recyclable materials that put together makes an unrecyclable format."No local authorities will accept these at the kerbside."If they end up at a sorting facility, they could end up contaminating the plastic stream because of the metals in there and that could be very problematic for plastics recyclers that get into the machinery."But why should people care if their drink packaging is not recyclable?Even the shape of the BuzzBallz make it harder to be recycled because they can roll on the conveyor belts at the sorting facilities, said Herriott.  Among the machinery used, scanners can identify it in one position, but by the time air jets are used to separate it into the right recycling stream, it could have moved, meaning it could contaminate other streams. "It's definitely one of the villains of recycling," said Ambarish Mitra, co-founder of Greyparrot, a waste analytics company which helps recovery facilities. He said BuzzBallz have "no recovery route in the current system" and are a "huge pet peeve for our customers and us".After analysing a plastic recover facility in Manchester with a processing capacity of 35,000 tonnes of plastic a year, for six months, the company found that BuzzBallz contaminated recycled plastic 66% of the time. "Once in the plastic stream, the aluminium reduces the quality of the recycled plastic, while the colour pigments can lower the recycled plastic bale's value."This isn't a recycling problem. It's a packaging problem."BuzzBallz refused to comment.James Piper, co-host of the Talking Rubbish podcast, co-owner of Ecosurety, said he dislikes BuzzBallz because of how difficult they are to recycle. "Every stage of the recycling journey has been designed around predictable packaging," Piper said. "When people come along and say, 'I'm going to make something different for marketing reasons', they are automatically making it more difficult for the recycler."There's nothing environmentally positive about mixing packaging types."He said the BuzzBallz 'biggies' which have a plastic screw top lid is completely recyclable."Anyone can say on their website 'this is recyclable where your council allows'. But if no council allows it, then it doesn't mean anything," he said. BuzzBallz said: "We very recently went through a global website update and the information pertaining to TerraCycle recycling for BuzzBallz was incorrectly copied and does not apply to the UK market as of today. "We apologise for the oversight and have since updated our website to reflect the correct position for UK consumers."The company refused to comment on the now-deleted UK FAQs stating its packaging was recyclable.

title: Fleeing a wall of flames: Tourists describe France wildfires escape
description: Tourists tell BBC how their holiday turned into race to escape firesImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Evacuation efforts are under way
body: Tourists tell BBC how their holiday turned into race to escape firesImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Evacuation efforts are under way in south-west FranceByEwan SomervilleUpdated 6 hours agoFamilies have relived how their tranquil holidays in France turned into a race to escape raging wildfires.Tourists told the BBC of emergency alerts in the middle of the night, desperate drives just metres from six-storey high flames and the sight of people flocking to beaches with their suitcases.Huge forest fires in south-west France and central Spain have displaced more than 220,000 people, with the French military drafted in to help and the Spanish government declaring a national emergency.Winds and continued heat are still helping to fan the flames with some tourists reporting smelling acrid smoke like a "bonfire" far outside the affected areas.Flights to Bordeaux and Madrid, the closest cities to the blaze-hit regions, are currently not affected. Earlier on Saturday, a French foreign minister described the fires as a "tragedy" but urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans.Among those caught up in the crisis is Zac Morrison, who arrived in Cap Ferret - a popular peninsula blanketed with pine trees 40 miles (65km) south-west of Bordeaux - on Thursday.The 21-year-old from London, who is on holiday with 10 members of his family, woke up to two text alerts at 04:00 and 06:00 local time ordering him to evacuate "by all means necessary".Image source, Andrea GrettonImage caption, A family showed the BBC how clouds of smoke descended on their campsite in Biscarrosse, south-west France"We had the gendarmerie [French military] going door to door," he told BBC Your Voice. "It was something like out of a movie - we had to take everything."Since experiencing "panic" before a "well organised" operation to clear out the entire peninsula, he said he received four different evacuation alerts from the authorities - the most recent at 17:00 on Friday - after "we moved away from one fire to only get put into the crosshairs of another".His family took shelter on a beach in nearby Arcachon before a relative came to their aid with a place to stay. His brother Nate, 11,  is still coming to terms with having seen the flames."Other people have been sleeping in schools and warehouses and the beaches have had people just waiting for the go ahead," Morrison added. "There's people on the beach here with their suitcases."He said the family was awaiting instructions on whether they can continue their holiday until mid August."It rained last night but we are hearing that electricity may be cut out over the peninsula, especially as the ash clouds go towards Bordeaux... I've heard about houses burning in just an hour, it's scary but sadly people here are getting used to it."Get in touchAre you in an affected region?  If it’s safe to do so, get in touch.Family fled in 15 minutesImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The wildfire on Moutchic beach on the shore of Lake LacanauDavid Morton, a headteacher, had enjoyed most of his week-long trip to Cap Ferret with his wife and two teenage sons in the forests under baking sun. But the mixture of "tinder dry" pine and intense heat helped upend things on day five when the family was awoken on Friday morning."Our phones were all flashing and bleeping; there was a message saying we had to evacuate immediately and drive on the one road out of the [Cap Ferret] peninsula," the 53-year-old said."We literally threw everything into our suitcases and within 15 minutes were in the hire car."He said they came within 500m of the main fire. "The flames were higher than full-size forest pine trees, so five or six storeys high, and it was clear this was a fire that was out of control at that point."The family, from Gloucestershire, has stayed with friends until their flight home from Bordeaux on Saturday.Image source, David MortonImage caption, David Morton's holiday was going smoothly until the final two days'City is evacuated but I'm still here'Others are still stranded. Rebecca Papin, a French-American visiting her holiday home in the commune of Biscarrosse, near to the Cap Ferret peninsula, saw a large plume of smoke in the distance on Thursday.Just three hours later when she arrived home that night, "there were water planes in the sky dropping water, firefighter helicopters in the sky and the entire distance was just a wall of flames," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme."It was quite far away from my house but I could see it very clearly from the upstairs level of my home."She said the authorities appeared "overwhelmed with trying" to fight the fire and issued no evacuation order, so she slept alongside her young children with her earplugs in - meaning she missed the sound of the evacuation overnight.Image source, David MortonImage caption, The flames seen from David Morton's car window"When I woke up in the morning we were almost alone in the city because the city has been evacuated and I'm still here," she said."The main roads are closed because they're on fire - the police advised me on Friday at 07:30 to stay in my home, to not leave my home under any circumstance; there was ash falling from the sky like snow."Some British families told the BBC they had moved 100 miles away to other parts of France to continue their holidays.Mark Dorey, from Leeds, decided to drive to the Dordogne with his wife and three children after being evacuated from a campsite near Parentis-en-Born."You wouldn't believe it, but me and my two boys were watching a Queen tribute act at the campsite bar - straight after a rendition of Bohemian Rhapsody someone stopped them to say we were being evacuated at about 22:00," he said.Image source, Mark DoreyImage caption, Mark Dorey and his family have changed locations in France to complete their holiday with more certaintyBefore heading to the Dordogne the family spent a night with hundreds of other evacuees in a gymnasium.Dorey, 42, said he feels lucky to be looked after and safe, but is thinking about holidaying "closer to home" next year.And BBC South's Joanna Kent, who was on holiday in the Cap Ferret peninsula earlier this week, recalled seeing her campsite deserted after two van loads of police told tourists they had 30 minutes to get out.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Shelters have been set up for evacuated residents and holidaymakersWhile the wildfires show no sign of abating soon, the UK Foreign Office is currently not advising against travel to France or Spain.Éléonore Caroit, France's minister for international partnerships, advised tourists on Saturday: "You have entire areas that are fine, you're seeing similar phenomena in Spain and other countries."I'm in Paris and nothing is happening, and most other regions are OK, so do please come to France and do not cancel your travel plans."But wherever you are, please do be advised as to what might be happening."In Madrid the fires are in the wider region far outside the city centre - and authorities are battling to stop different fires merging.But the flames have already shut down a facility for US space agency Nasa 37 miles (65km) west of the city.Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described the fire there as the "worst fire in the history of the region", with the area facing a "perfect storm" of high temperatures, relentless wind and merging fire fronts.Additional reporting by: James Kelly, Rozina Sini, Alex Akhurst and Mary Litchfield

schema.headline: Fleeing a wall of flames: Tourists describe France wildfires escape

title: Police investigate donations by Richard Tice company to Reform UK
description: Police are investigating payments to Reform UK by a company controlled by the party's deputy leader, Richard Tice, BBC News has learned.Britain Means
body: Police are investigating payments to Reform UK by a company controlled by the party's deputy leader, Richard Tice, BBC News has learned.Britain Means Business gave the party two donations of £250,000 in the run-up to the 2024 general election, when Tice was party chairman. Tice has said the money was given to his firm by Fiona Cottrell, a significant donor to Reform UK and mother of a convicted fraudster with close links to Nigel Farage.Tice said: "This is the first I have heard of it - if true why are the Met Police briefing the BBC before contacting interested parties? Is the Met leadership now engaged in the widespread politically motivated smear campaign against Reform and its leaders?"Earlier this month, the Times newspaper, external revealed that two donations given directly by Fiona Cottrell to Reform UK in May 2024 were being investigated by the Metropolitan Police.That investigation relates to legislation governing elections, which bans concealing or disguising donations derived from an "impermissible" donor, or the use of "false" information about a donation including the amount or the identity of the donor.The BBC has asked Fiona Cottrell for comment.Britain Means Business, which is solely owned and controlled by Tice, received £1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.Disclosures to the Electoral Commission show that the company then donated a total of £500,000 to Reform UK in the same month.Tice told the BBC earlier this month that it was entirely his choice for the company to give half of the money from Fiona Cottrell to his party.The payments came to light when the Guardian newspaper, external revealed they had been flagged to the National Crime Agency as part of its Suspicious Activity Reports programme.Now BBC News has learned that they are part of the Met's investigation into donations to Reform UK.The BBC understands that the party was not aware of the investigation into the payments from Britain Means Business.A Reform UK spokesman said: "Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with donations so far."Fiona Cottrell's son, George Cottrell, has been at the centre of a political row in recent weeks.The Sunday Times has reported he supported Farage by paying for staff and security before the 2024 election, but these benefits were not declared once Farage became an MP. Farage has since stepped down as an MP and is standing for re-election in the constituency of Clacton.Farage has consistently argued any money given to him before he was elected an MP came in a personal capacity and therefore did not need to be declared. Lawyers for Cottrell have said he "categorically disputes allegations and assertions made by The Sunday Times, which clearly fail to reflect what that publisher was told in advance of its reporting".Asked by the Sunday Times if Cottrell had transferred money to his mother before she made donations to Reform UK, his lawyers at Carter Ruck said: "Our client has confirmed his instructions that any donations by his mother have been entirely her own decision."George Cottrell has long been a close political and personal ally of the Reform UK leader.He pleaded guilty to fraud in the United States and spent eight months in jail there, before being released in 2017.Upon his release he moved back to the UK and now lives in Montenegro.At a rally in Norfolk on Tuesday Nigel Farage said he had "absolutely no idea" whether George Cottrell had given money to his mother to donate onwards to the party, adding, "What's it got to do with me how families sort out their finances?""If the money was hers legally and she gave the donation, I don't see what the problem is," he said.Britain Means Business was set up in August 2017 under the name Leave Means Leave and campaigned for a "clean Brexit".The organisation was set up by Tice and John Longworth, a former boss of the British Chambers of Commerce and prominent Brexit campaigner.Longworth left Leave Means Leave in January 2020, the month the UK officially left the EU.A few months later Tice changed the organisation's name to Britain Means Business. He now solely owns and controls the business.

schema.headline: Police investigate donations by Richard Tice company to Reform UK

title: Tour de France 2026: Tadej Pogacar set for record fifth win
description: Tadej Pogacar is set to secure a record-equalling fifth Tour de France after a dramatic stage 20 saw Ecuador's Richard Carapaz clinch victory on Alpe
body: Tadej Pogacar is set to secure a record-equalling fifth Tour de France after a dramatic stage 20 saw Ecuador's Richard Carapaz clinch victory on Alpe d'Huez as Sepp Kuss crashed twice while leading in the last few kilometres.If Pogacar avoids a race-ending crash on Sunday's final stage to Paris, in which the overall standings are traditionally not contested, he will become the joint-most successful rider in the Tour's history alongside Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain.Pogacar, 27, of UAE Team Emirates-XRG, finished the three-week Grand Tour's 'queen' stage in fourth place after helping his 22-year-old Mexican team-mate Isaac del Toro provisionally seal third place on the overall podium and the young rider classification's white jersey. The pair crossed the line together with their arms around each other's shoulders after Pogacar paced a suffering Del Toro up the final climb.Pogacar will claim his fifth overall yellow jersey in Paris by six minutes and 26 seconds over Belgium's Remco Evenepoel of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, after Evenepoel finished the stage in second, 26 seconds behind Carapaz, after a late charge."I did my best to help Isaac," said Pogacar afterwards. "Massive respect for what all the guys have been doing in the past three weeks. I finally experienced [being a domestique] myself and I already before appreciate [the] work of team-mates, but now it's like another level."It was goosebumps [as we crossed the line together]. [It] was fantastic and one for the memories."On his future, he added: "I definitely will not be doing this for too much [of a] long time, I think. Isaac showed great potential, but we don't put any pressure yet on Isaac." Race organisers ASO announced during the stage that Sunday's finale will have its distance reduced from 133km to 89km after the redirection of emergency services to help tackle devastating wildfires in the south-west of the country. Traditionally, the final stage sees the sport's sprinters battle for the line on the famous Champs Elysees cobbles, but a new section over Montmartre allows riders with more sustained power the potential to steal a breakaway win.The most demanding stage of the whole race was left to the penultimate day, in which riders had to climb 5,450 metres across three hors category climbs covering 170.9km to finish in the iconic Alpe d'Huez ski-resort for a second time in two days. American Kuss of Visma-Lease a Bike was part a large early breakaway which contained riders looking for a stage win, and attacked alone with about 25km to go.The 31-year-old looked to have found the strength which helped him win the Vuelta a Espana in 2023 and seemed set to hold on to a slender lead for victory. But the often unflappable Kuss was on the ragged edge and crashed coming out of a tunnel approaching Alpe d'Huez town. He maintained his lead, but soon after crashed again on a right-hand corner after getting his line wrong, his rear wheel sliding on dust at the edge of the road before coming to a stop, half off his bike and leaning into safety netting which prevented him from falling down a sheer drop.The tenacious Carapaz, of EF Education-Easypost, swept past Kuss and into the lead - the 2019 Giro d'Italia winner, eventually taking his second stage win in three days and also securing victory in the king of the mountains competition."[I was] not really scared," Kuss told TNT Sports afterwards. "I was just annoyed because we drove down it this morning and I looked at that corner and thought: 'Ah that's a pretty descent corner, no problem in the race,' so I took it pretty full-on. "It was a bit more of a corner than I expected. My wife won't let me race my bike anymore - she always tells me not take risks on the downhills, but you've got to have a little adrenaline rush every once in a while."Typically, on a stage such as this one in the French Alps, Pogacar would be expected to deliver yet another masterclass but he held back to help Del Toro, who at one point was starting to struggle on the Col du Galibier, to defend his white jersey and third place overall from French sensation Paul Seixas of Decathlon CMA-CGM.The 19-year-old Seixas finally ran out of energy on the final mountain of the race and is set to finish fourth in the general classification, 11 minutes and 56 seconds down on Pogacar's overall time.Britain's Tom Pidcock of Pinarello-Q36.5 finished the stage 16th, nine minutes and three seconds down, and will finish ninth overall in the GC.Denmark's Mads Pedersen of Lidl-Trek will win the green points jersey in Paris on Sunday just by finishing as he leads Belgium's Jasper Philipsen of Alpecin-Premier Tech by an uncatchable 82 points. title: Hungarian Grand Prix: Lando Norris cautious despite pole as qualifying 'falls apart' for Lewis Hamilton
description: Lando Norris took his first pole position of the year in Hungary but is cautious about whether he can follow it up with his first victory as world cha
body: Lando Norris took his first pole position of the year in Hungary but is cautious about whether he can follow it up with his first victory as world champion.Perhaps the McLaren driver was casting his mind back to Miami in early May, when he was leading towards the end of the first stint of the race, only for his team to make a strategic misstep and allow Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli to sneak in for a win."You can't just rely on one good qualifying, so I need a good race tomorrow," Norris said."Then we obviously have a nice summer break, but after that we need to try and repeat it several more times."We've been working hard. We know we've been on the back foot, but we're making progress and today certainly shows that."Much of the attention at the Hungarian Grand Prix has been on the massive upgrade made by Aston Martin on their recalcitrant car, which has provided the troubled team with a major step forward and allowed Fernando Alonso to escape the first qualifying session for the first time all season.That meant McLaren's own upgrade went under the radar somewhat, but it has been effective.Still, team principal Andrea Stella, while expressing his satisfaction that the upgrades had enabled them to engage in a fight for pole they did not expect, said Norris' pole was an "overachievement".McLaren's own good execution of qualifying was one factor, he said, in addition to  an under-performance from Ferrari, and perhaps even Antonelli and Mercedes.Ferrari came into Hungary as most people's favourite, including McLaren's, on the basis that their car is the fastest in the corners, but it lacks engine performance, and this is one of the least power-sensitive tracks on the calendar.Lewis Hamilton was fastest after the first runs in the final part of qualifying but did not improve on his final lap. Shortly after completing it, he blocked Norris' team-mate Oscar Piastri and the stewards imposed a three-place grid penalty.Ferrari boss Frederic Vasseur said the team took responsibility for that because they did not warn Hamilton in time.The seven-time world champion later posted on Instagram:, external "Sometimes you just can't catch a break. Another weekend when I've been feeling great throughout all the sessions, but then it just falls apart."Referencing penalties he had been given in the previous two races in Britain and Belgium, Hamilton added: "I always do my best to keep positive - sport is always about the highs and lows, but it's also in the margins."Every point counts and you have to seize every opportunity. After three penalties in three weekends, it's becoming difficult to hang on to that positivity. "Still, I won't let the setbacks take away from the progress we've been making as a team. With the pace we have, I'm hopeful we can get something out of the race tomorrow."For all that Ferrari have been quick, Norris and McLaren have also looked in good shape all weekend. And, at least on this circuit, they have vaulted right to the front, into a position that had been familiar for the past two seasons but not so in 2026.While sat with Ferrari's Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, Norris said: "I knew the pace was certainly there. It has been all weekend. Even though these guys have been insanely fast, I knew I'd been driving very well, I'd been consistent, and I knew the car had potential. "We also had the upgrades this weekend, and it doesn't feel that different, but it certainly seems to be going a little bit quicker, and that's always a good thing." Overtaking is expected to be especially difficult around the Hungaroring this year. In Miami an excess of caution on McLaren's part about the potential of rain allowed Mercedes to pit Antonelli before Norris and leap into the lead.Norris' pole provides an opportunity to make amends for that - if he can keep Leclerc behind on the run to the first corner.After winning two consecutive constructors' titles in 2024 and 2025, as well as Norris' drivers' championship last year, McLaren have not had a great season at the start of this new regulation cycle.Securing the title against a late-season onslaught from Max Verstappen and Red Bull put them behind on designing this year's car, and they took some missteps on aerodynamic philosophy that only became fully understood after the first handful of races.An upgrade package introduced by McLaren this weekend, their first since Miami, is the fruit of work aimed at correcting course, and the first signs are positive.They have also struggled to get on top of the operation of the new Mercedes engine, feeling for the first time that they were suffering for not being a works partner of a manufacturer."It's just nice to be on pole," said Norris, who had also shown competitive pace in Belgium last weekend but was denied a good result by a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding the permitted number of engine parts, and then by bad luck with the timing of a safety car."I have felt good all weekend. The last few weekends, honestly, I felt pretty good and it's been nice I continued my good feelings in the car."I had my money on Ferrari before the weekend and they have been insanely quick, but, come qualifying, we just seemed to take more of a step forward. I knew it was possible and that has been a good feeling - and one that I have missed for quite a while."As for his prospects in the race, Norris alluded to strong performances from the Mercedes and Ferrari drivers on the race-simulation runs in Friday practice when he said: "The race pace on others looked very strong. It is always a bit tricky to know how things will go with a new car and new bits."Leclerc, though, felt Norris would certainly be in the fight, and both have some protection from Hamilton and Antonelli, both demoted by three-place penalties to fifth and seventh respectively."Lando seems to be very, very strong, so I'll say Lando [is favourite]," Leclerc said. "But if you look over the course of the season, Mercedes has always been up there, so I do not doubt that they'll all be in the fight as well."At Aston Martin there was at last some reason to feel positive after a dark time this season.So much had been expected of the team when design legend Adrian Newey joined in March last year, but a late start to their design process, combined with engine partner Honda falling well short of performance and - like McLaren - some errors in philosophy, have left them cemented at the back all year.In absolute terms, progressing beyond the first session for the first time all season, and lining up 16th, is nothing special. But to be able to compete with other teams, for pretty much the first time all year, was a major step.In percentage terms, this was not quite Aston Martin's best performance of the season - they were 0.012% closer to pole in Japan. But it is huge compared with where they have fallen since as others have developed their cars.There is a Honda engine upgrade to come for the next race after the summer break - of undefined size. More importantly, this has revitalised faith in Aston Martin's development capabilities after three years of upgrades that failed to deliver what the team expected."There is more potential to unlock in the car, but it's normal when you have such a big package," Alonso said."It was important for everyone in the team as it has been a tough period in both factories."Having the deficit that we had in terms of performance in the first half of the year and this package, it didn't change many positions, but it changed a lot the momentum of everyone in the factory."It's not any more that we are chasing something that we don't know. We know exactly what we are looking for and we know exactly the targets for the next package or the targets for next year. So that's for me the biggest change of this weekend."Whether it is enough for Alonso to decide to commit to another season behind the wheel remains to be seen.He turns 45 next week. He has said he still feels competitive - and continues to prove it. But he is no fan of the energy management required from this year's engines.He continues to profess his confidence that Newey and Honda will eventually produce the best car and engine. But, as he keeps repeating, the question is how long that will take, and whether it fits his timeline.As he said upon arriving in Hungary on Thursday: "It's not a problem with the competitiveness of the team. It's just a problem of whether Formula 1 gives me the adrenaline that I need to live."Alonso has a lot of thinking to do as he heads off on his summer break - his first as a father - next week.

schema.headline: Hungarian Grand Prix: Lando Norris cautious despite pole as qualifying 'falls apart' for Lewis Hamilton

title: More than 250,000 evacuated as wildfires rage in France and Spain
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Firefighters battle flames in Lège-Cap-Ferret, south-western FranceByDearbail Jordan and Sofia Ferreira SantosUpdated
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Firefighters battle flames in Lège-Cap-Ferret, south-western FranceByDearbail Jordan and Sofia Ferreira SantosUpdated 3 hours agoFirefighters are struggling to contain wildfires in south-west France as strong winds push flames towards the city of Bordeaux, with one official saying they "are far from having the fire under control."More than 250,000 people in France and Spain have fled fires which have been raging for days, as winds and high temperatures hamper efforts to contain them. Overnight, seven towns west of Bordeaux were told to evacuate residents. In Spain, where a state of emergency has been declared, a change in weather conditions has helped firefighters outside Madrid.Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez admitted there are "complex times ahead". Meanwhile, authorities in València confirmed the death of a man in a fire.The man, believed to be in his 70s, was found dead in his car by firefighters as they extinguished a fire in the Salt de l'Aigua ravine in Manises, according to local media reports.In France, around 200,000 people have been evacuated in south-western regions of Gironde and Landes regions.France has mobilised its military to help with the response and extra reinforcements from the army have been sent to help firefighters by clearing brush and creating fire breaks.As of Saturday morning, the wildfire was around 40km to 50km (25 to 30 miles) away from Bordeaux. Still, the wind was blowing smoke towards the city and people reported an acrid smell in the air.One tourist who fled an approaching wildfire near Bordeaux with his family described the scale of the blaze as "frightening".Spencer Randall told the BBC his family evacuated in the early hours of Saturday to an area 100 miles east, but they can "still smell the wildfires from here"."It's quite strong winds fanning the flames, just terrifying," he said.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Shelters have been set up across the region to house evacueesA British couple holidaying in Bordeaux said they noticed the flames get worse on Friday night, as the fire approached."At about seven o'clock you could smell smoke. We thought someone was having a barbecue," Maisie told BBC Newsbeat from their holiday rental.Her partner, Caleb, said the ash has now covered the pool in the house and turned their feet black when walking outside.The smoke "really hits your lungs right away", they added.Nearby, in Saint-Aubin-de-Médoc, residents evacuating said the situation was "stressful", with one local describing it a "disaster".The final leg of the Tour de France, due to take place Sunday, has been shortened from 133km (83 miles) to 89km (55 miles) so that security forces can be redeployed to areas affected by wildfires, organisers and police have said.French President Emmanuel Macron is set to have an emergency meeting with ministers as 30 or so fires rage across the country - a situation which the government said is totally unprecedented.Figure caption, Watch: Anxiety as locals forced to evacuate Saint-Aubin-de-MédocIn Spain, fires continued near Madrid but the regional government said there had been some progress."The change in weather conditions - less wind, higher humidity and lower temperature - has greatly benefited the fight against the forest fires, which have advanced little and decreased in intensity," it wrote on X.Speaking from Cenicientos, south-west of Madrid, Prime Minister Sánchez said: "Right now, we have a window of opportunity in order to tackle against the wildfires, protect and save lives and effectively try and control the fire.""It's true that temperatures have dropped a little bit. But still the wind is making it difficult and there may be thunderstorms as well." Since the wildfires broke out in Spain, nearly 60,000 people have been evacuated from the Madrid and Ávila regions, while more than 28,000 remain confined to their homes, according to Spain's Interior Ministry.Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described the situation as the "worst fire in the history of the region".Sánchez said 130,000 hectares of land had been burned in Spain so far this year, ahead of an annual average of 100,000 hectares for the country over the last decade.  Image source, Cesar MANSO / AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, A helicopter dumps water as firefighters collect water from a pool in El Tiemblo, outside MadridFrance's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 98,000 hectares have burned across the country since the beginning of 2026.Meanwhile in Italy, more than 350 fires - including 10 major blazes - broke out on the island of Sicily, the head of the Sicilian Civil Protection said on Wednesday, prompting evacuations.A major incident was also declared by emergency services in Scotland on Friday evening as they continue to tackle a wildfire in the Cairngorms National Park that has been burning for 10 days.Hadja Lahbib, the EU's commissioner for crisis management, said it is likely that the damage from wildfires in Europe will surpass previous records.Figure caption, Watch: Flames reach evacuated town outside MadridShe said fires had started earlier in the year when, in April, the Netherlands activated the EU's civil protection mechanism which triggers support and reinforcements from other countries.Lahbib told the BBC: "Last year, one million hectares burned during the summer and so we are expecting to face another historical, sad record because the season has started earlier in the year."She also warned that more outbreaks are likely as the summer goes on. "Forecasters are predicting, unfortunately, another heatwave so we can expect other wildfires," Lahbib added.France has activated the civil protection mechanism and will receive water bombers, comprising three Canadairs planes from Croatia and two Air Tractors from Portugal, as well as Black Hawk helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia, and 40 members of a Romanian forest fire team.EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said 11 planes and helicopters have also been sent to France and Spain from the EU's firefighting fleet.Additional reporting by Mary Litchfield, BBC Your Voice and Srosh Khan, BBC Newsbeat

schema.headline: More than 250,000 evacuated as wildfires rage in France and Spain

title: Who could be the next Graham Norton, and does the BBC even need one?
description: Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?Image caption, Winkleman stepped down from her chat show last
body: Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?Image caption, Winkleman stepped down from her chat show last week following its seven-episode runBySteven McIntoshEntertainment reporterWhen Lisa Kudrow appeared on The Claudia Winkleman Show earlier this year, she was visibly delighted to meet Linda from The Traitors. The Friends actress, probably the most famous guest the programme had during its seven-week run, said it was "thrilling" to meet one of the reality show's breakout stars, who she revealed had even inspired one of her own recent performances.As host of The Traitors, Winkleman was ideally placed to introduce the pair, resulting in the kind of wonderfully bizarre meeting of minds normally seen on The Graham Norton Show. But Winkleman's own chat show did not last long enough for any more unusual guest combinations on its teal sofa. The presenter quit last week after just one series, saying she was simply "too nervous to enjoy it". It had made sense for the BBC to commission The Claudia Winkleman Show, given the presenter's popularity on programmes such as Strictly.There's a different level of pressure, however, hosting a show with your own name above the door. Image caption, Lisa Kudrow (second left) said she was "thrilled" to meet Linda from the Traitors (far right) on the chat show"Everyone thought she could pull it off because she's smart and funny, but a chat show with multiple guests is very difficult to handle," the Telegraph's arts and entertainment editor, Anita Singh, tells BBC News."You have to marshall the conversation, give each guest equal time, help them to plug whatever they're plugging, then cue in whatever anecdote they've agreed beforehand with the researchers. Graham Norton makes that look deceptively easy."She adds: "I think if Claudia had done a couple more series she would have become better at it. But she's at her best when she's being spontaneous, and the format allows very little space for that."Winkleman's decision to quit surprised many. The viewing figures were lower than Norton's, but still respectable. The reviews from critics were mixed, rather than universally bad. The BBC confirmed it was Winkleman's decision to stop, and implied that they would've happily commissioned a second series - and possibly already had. "My understanding is they had made a deal beyond one season," says Deadline's Jake Kanter, who has reported on the talk show throughout. "How formal that was, I don't know. But there was an intention for it to continue."He adds: "I wholeheartedly believe her that this perhaps didn't work out because of her own concerns and anxiety around the hosting."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Winkleman's chat show was made by Graham Norton's production company So TelevisionFormer BBC One controller Peter Fincham, who hosts the TV podcast Insiders, likens it to the Davina McCall chat show he commissioned in 2006, which also ended after one series. "You have to remember, particularly chat shows where the presenter's name is in the title, it's very exposing for them," he tells BBC News. "Had Claudia Winkleman wanted to carry on with her chat show, it could have been a slow burn," he reflects. "But what she's done is rare, actually, for somebody to say, 'hmm, didn't really enjoy that, don't think I'll do it again'. "That says something very positive about her that you don't often see among presenters."Succession planningMany considered Winkleman, 54, to be chat show emperor Graham Norton's presumptive successor - not least because he seemed to be ushering her through himself.So Television, which Norton co-owns, also produced Winkleman's show, and it could have been a neat way for the company to retain work when Norton does eventually quit.Admittedly, Norton's show is not vanishing any time soon - he signed a new three-year deal with the BBC in 2025. He has also taken on several new projects, including a podcast, more novels, and a short-lived ITV game show, The Neighbourhood.But Norton, 63, has also spoken openly in recent years about working less. He reduced the number of chat show episodes he presents in 2022, and also stepped down from his Virgin Radio show two years later.Image source, BBC/So TelevisionImage caption, The BBC signed a new three-year deal with The Graham Norton Show in 2025The short life of The Claudia Winkleman Show could make the Norton succession plan a key issue for the BBC's incoming entertainment chief, Ed Havard. "This does leave the BBC with a problem if and when Graham decides to retire, because if Claudia can't do it, I don't know who can," says Singh."Graham doesn't want to do 52 weeks a year," Fincham notes, "so I'm sure the BBC would have been delighted to have another long-running chat show that you can balance with his, and they may have another try."Dozens of presenters would love the gig and many would be perfectly capable - Jack Whitehall did a solid job when he stood in for Norton previously, or Alan Carr could probably be tempted to return to his Chatty Man days. But the TV landscape is also littered with examples of cancelled chat shows. As well as Winkleman and McCall, Lily Allen and Charlotte Church also hosted series which didn't last long. Image caption, Winkleman will continue to host The Traitors and the forthcoming second series of its popular celebrity spin-offA cynic might say that the short life of Winkleman's series will have shown both her and the BBC that launching a new chat show is harder than it looks.But Kanter has a more nuanced interpretation, reflecting: "My instinct is that this was always a bit of an experiment. "Clearly it was something that Claudia wanted to do, and when you have a presenter at the peak of her powers, I think it's just good talent management to try and work together with that presenter on their dream project."He adds: "I'm sure all sides will walk away with their heads held high, and it was worth giving it a crack, I think."Do we still need chat shows?Personalities aside, there's the more existential question of whether the BBC even needs a new talk series, when there are now hundreds of other platforms where celebrities can go to promote their product. Stars can just as easily appear on YouTube strands such as Snack Wars or Hot Ones as a TV chat show, or spend as much time at press junkets being interviewed by TikTokers as legacy media outlets. Talent agents know that seeing Hollywood stars talking to a lovable and sweary East London pensioner, external known as Grime Gran, or playing a game of Would You Rather, external with LadBible, is just as likely to generate publicity as traditional interviews.Singh highlights that clips from programmes such as Norton's often go viral too, but adds: "I don't think the public is craving another TV chat show."Think back to the most memorable encounters from the heyday of chat shows," she says. "They were one-on-one: Parkinson with Muhammad Ali; Wogan with George Best or David Icke. "Those long-form interviews have moved to podcasts now, where celebrities find it easy to be open and essentially treat them as an extended therapy session. "And the most entertaining celebrity interviews around are on Amelia Dimoldenberg's Chicken Shop Date. Compared to content like that, a chat show in a TV studio seems quite old-fashioned."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dimoldenberg interviews stars on Chicken Shop Date and now serves as the Oscars' red carpet reporterNorton's show clearly still delivers huge value for the BBC, and Kanter says the "chat show format remains strong" and is a "really important part of the BBC One schedule"."It sprinkles a bit of stardust, it's appointment to view, I think people enjoy that it's a Friday night and they can tune in for some entertainment, it performs well online, it's an engine for clips and viral moments, and that's something that's to be valued in this attention economy," he notes.And, speaking from experience, Fincham concludes he is "not a big fan of succession plans" anyway."I ran BBC One between 2005 and 2007," he recalls, "and at that time, a regular conversation was 'What's the succession plan for David Attenborough?' "That was 20 years ago, and I can't help noticing he's still presenting programmes today. So beware of the assumption that a succession plan is needed. "And Graham Norton, if he chooses to continue, has got plenty more in the tank."

schema.headline: Who could be the next Graham Norton, and does the BBC even need one?

title: 'The dogs were getting upset': How LA band Muna survived their worst ever gig
description: The pop band who went from playing for rescue dogs to selling out arenasImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Muna's concert for rescue dogs didn't
body: The pop band who went from playing for rescue dogs to selling out arenasImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Muna's concert for rescue dogs didn't go according to planByMusic correspondentEvery band has to earn its stripes. Some have it harder than others.At AC/DC's first gig, the club owner cut the power because they were too noisy. Sam Smith started at barn dances, singing on top of a haystack. At Robert Smith's first concert, he got so drunk that he sang David Bowie's Suffragette City while the rest of the band played Jimi Hendrix's Foxy Lady.But LA pop trio Muna can top them all.At the start of their career, the band got a call from their record label. We know you've just flown overnight from London, they said, but you have to get to Las Vegas.Why? Because they'd been booked to play Pet-A-Palooza, a dog adoption festival sponsored by the local radio station. If they turned up, the station would support their new single."We were all sick, so it was doomed from the start," recalls guitarist Josette Maskin."It was an acoustic set, but we didn't have a sound guy, and the guitar started feeding back."The noise, according to singer Katie Gavin, was like an unholy screech."The dogs were getting upset," says Maskin, wincing at the memory. "They just howled the whole time."We were mortified, but looking back, it is so funny. And I've gotten to share those experiences with some of my best friends, and that's what life is really about."Image source, Dean BradshawImage caption, Muna in 2026 (L-R): Naomi McPherson, Katie Gavin and Josette MaskinNowadays, that canine catastrophe is a dot in Muna's rear-view mirror. Over the past decade, they've become one of the most compelling live bands around – a little bit punk, a little bit electronic, a little bit 80s, eminently watchable and endlessly impressive.Fans include Harry Styles and Taylor Swift, who handpicked the trio (completed by guitarist/producer Naomi McPherson) to support them on tour.They were won over by sing-along anthems like I Know A Place, a great big exuberant hug for the LGBTQ community; and the more introspective Stayaway, where Gavin locks herself in her bedroom to avoid anything - friends, music, drink - that could tempt her back into the arms of an ex.In 2020, all their momentum nearly came to a crashing halt when RCA Records dropped the band, citing pandemic-era cost-cutting."That's obviously one where we had to put our heads together and be like, 'OK, we want to continue doing this. Let's just make an album and we'll figure it out'," says McPherson.'We need movement'That album, simply titled Muna, was eventually released by indie star Phoebe Bridgers, who swooped in to sign the band to her Saddest Factory label in 2021."Phoebe's manager had made it very clear that if we were ever single, she'd be interested in working with us," Gavin told the BBC at the time.Bridgers also provided guest vocals on Silk Chiffon, a freewheeling sapphic love song that became Muna's breakthrough single.It pegged the band, in its members' own words, as "the queer joy mini-skirt rollerblade, external" crew - but their music has always dug deeper than that.I Know A Place, for example, was written as a response to the 2016 Pulse nightclub shooting, acknowledging the fragility of the communal LGBTQ spaces it celebrated.Their fourth album, Dancing On The Wall, is their most powerful yet.The music is darker. The lyrics hit harder. Ostensibly anchored to the dancefloor, it's a record that uses dance music to shake the listener out of complacency."I think it was a response to a feeling of helplessness in this moment in time that can lead to paralysis," says Gavin."Movement is what we need right now, and we also need to feel powerful and to connect to our sources of energy. The tempo of this album helps with that."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The band are best seen live: "We were super lucky to hit at the right time to be able to play tiny venues and work our way up to where we are now," says McPhersonThe standout, lyrically speaking, is Big Stick. A critique of American imperialism, it's written from the perspective of Big Brother, who "can make you want anything that I want you to" – from war in Gaza to the militarisation of US police forces."And If you've got a problem with it, you could end up in jail," Gavin seethes as militaristic synths patrol the beat."I think sometimes people want to go to concerts to feel a brief reprieve from the horrors of the world around them, but right now the horrors are so pervasive that what I found myself wanting was a container to express my anger together with other people," says the singer."It's an emotional release that I think we are often denied because we have to read tragedies in the news every day and then keep our heads down and work."Given the polarised state of political discourse in the US, did they have any misgivings about releasing the song?"Maybe this is actually stupid, but I don't think it was a big decision for us," says Maskin."We have always been a political band, and we've always been super open with what we believe in, so it really wasn't a question."Elsewhere, the album transports the listener to sweaty, laser-lit nightclubs, where unyielding rhythms fuel feelings of "horniness and heartache".The title track is full of thwarted desire, as Gavin tries and fails to get the attention of a girl who constantly leaves her dangling. Wannabeher, meanwhile, is a sticky, sleazy track about being so completely besotted with someone that you start to blur the boundaries between where your personality ends and theirs begins."I think that's a canon gay experience, where you don't know whether you want to be with someone or you actually want to be them," laughs Maskin.Image caption, The band formed at university in 2013, with McPherson producing all of their musicEastside Girls, meanwhile, is a tender depiction of Muna's neighbourhood, lovingly lampooning the staples of LA hipster culture – astrology, polyamory, roommate dramas and "negronis with the nice gin"."It's a city that's run by sunshine," says McPherson, who moved to LA from her native San Diego."It's bohemian but it's also populated by some of the richest people in the world. It's a strange dichotomy."The song's chorus is a masterclass in melody and, in Maskin's words, "smacks you in the face". It takes its place among Muna's most irresistible hooks (see also, Number One Fan, Stayaway, What I Want) – which all stem from Gavin's love of classic pop."She's been writing songs since she was eight years old, so it's a well-honed skill," says McPherson."I think it's a benefit of my obsessive personality, honestly," says Gavin."I am constantly searching for the next big chorus, and will probably always be. Also, once I have a seed in my head for a song that feels promising, it really has a hold on me and won't let me go until I feel I've done it justice." (Wannabeher, McPherson reveals, is the final version of a song that began 11 years ago.)"I will say," Gavin adds, "one random tip is writing in motion - walking, driving, rollerblading, anything like that."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Muna's tour hits the UK this November, in their biggest venues to dateThat explains why Muna's music always feels propulsive. "If you're not sweating after the first song, come on," laughs McPherson.With an ever-growing fanbase, they'll play their biggest ever tour this autumn, titled the Gets So Hot Tour after the album's opening track – although the band previously joked it would be called "The Midwest Princess, Midnight Sun and the Eras Tour as Well", before abandoning the idea for copyright reasons.A decade into their career, they're playing to "crowds we could never have imagined", while witnessing the genre labelled as "queer pop" expand into the mainstream, with artists like Chappell Roan, Renée Rapp, Lil Nas X and Troye Sivan all achieving crossover success."I do feel we were at the cusp of the reclamation of the word 'queer'," says Maskin."To us, it's actually a celebratory term, because it's inclusive, it includes everybody in the LGBTQI+ community."It came from academia first, the idea of queer theory," says McPherson, who admits the band were initially divided on whether to be open about their sexuality."We were reticent to come out of the closet in the hipster Pitchfork era of 2010 and 2011. We wanted to be mysterious and be closeted, and Katie was the one who encouraged us not to, and to just be ourselves. And we've only become more ourselves."Even so, the label can be restrictive. Muna want their music to be universal."The subject matter we write about is queer in its essence, and so are our life experiences," says McPherson."The issue that we struggle with is wanting that to also be accepted as just a human experience, as well – especially in these times of great repression."If anyone can do it, Muna can. Just don't let them play for your pets.
